speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PRICES AND SUPPLY-MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it desirable to make a statement to the house in regard to the supply and price of farm implements. Throughout the war years, and continuing through to the present, the question of ensuring an adequate, supply of farm implements is one which has consistently been given special attention by the government. Towards the end of 1941 when the needs of war caused acute shortages of steel and component parts, hon. members will recall that a rigid control and allocation of all forms of steel and components was found necessary and a far-reaching priority system was set up. When doing so, however, particular attention was given to the needs for farm implements and they were placed in the very special position of receiving a priority as high as essential war production in regard to production programmes agreed upon from time to time. A special international committee was formed cpmprising representatives from the United States, United Kingdom and Canada to screen the requirements of the allied nations for farm machinery and equipment so as to determine minimum essential needs in relation to agreed food programmes. This committee worked out the allocation of available materials for each country aqd maintained a fair balance in its distribution. When this had been accomplished it became the responsibility of each country to determine what machines and equipment were produced to meet essential needs.
Through these special measures hon. members will be interested to know that despite the most urgent pressures for direct war equipment the government was successful in providing for Canada a steady flow of farm implements throughout the course of the war.
Notwithstanding this fact, however, it is true that a greatly expanded agricultural production, obtained despite a serious decline in farm labour, has meant that the demand for machinery and equipment continues far in excess of available supply. A significant barometer of the demand in this field has been the fact that in farm auction sales, prices bid for used machinery and equipment have been often far in excess of maximum ceiling prices on new equipment.
[The Governor General.]
Immediately following the cessation of hostilities the question of diverting all possible industrial production facilities towards meeting the demand for farm machinery and equipment was taken energetically in hand. The urgent need for food is so apparent that I need not emphasize it. Suffice it to say that it is the obvious duty of all producing countries to increase agricultural production to a maximum and all practical steps toward this end must be taken.
In studying the measures necessary to secure a maximum production of farm machinery and equipment the wartime prices and trade board, to whose administrative jurisdiction this question is entrusted, has reached the conclusion that some recognition of the uncontrollable war-time increases in the cost of materials, labour and general overhead is simply inevitable if vitally needed machineiy and implements are to be secured. This decision was reached after a careful study of cost information submitted by the farm implement industry. Accordingly, on Saturday, April 13, the board announced that maximum retail price ceilings for Canadian-made farm machinery and parts will be increased by twelve and a half per cent. Naturally, this step was taken with considerable reluctance. However, faced with the plain fact that increased costs of materials and component parts produced in Canada, or imported for assembly here, together with increased labour and other overhead costs, could not be absorbed at present price levels, it was obvious that a maximum production of farm machinery and equipment could not take place unless some relief was afforded. I/should add that the analysis of costs conducted by the prices board indicated that a price increase of upwards of 30 per cent above 1941 levels would have been required to regain 1941 profit percentage margins for the farm implement industry. Consequently, the price advance of only 12i per cent means, admittedly, a serious profit squeeze upon the industry, but in this transition period the government believes the prices board approach in the case of farm implements to be fully justified in view of the imperative need for holding down to a minimum, cost adjustments in the important basic industry of agriculture.
With one minor exception of a 5 per cent increase to adjust an anomalous situation on a small volume of implements (principally imported items) at the commencement of the price ceiling in the fall of 1941, prices have been held at or below the ceiling prices of the basic period in 1941. This rather remarkable record was made possible partly by

Farm Implements
reason of large war contracts which expanded the volume of the industry and partly by insisting that increasing costs be absorbed by the industry instead of being passed on to the farmer consumer. Now that war production has swung over to normal supplies, however, the cost increases, as I have already stated, can no longer be absorbed and a reasonable price adjustment had to be worked out. In their submissions the companies disclosed increased costs since the basic period of 1941 averaging, roughly, materials and components 20 per cent, labour 28-J per cent, and general overhead 23 per cent. Unit costs in the coming year will run higher than this for some time due to premiums on castings, increases on imported components and higher than normal overheads which bring the over-all cost increase close to 30 per cent. In fixing the increase in the ceiling price at not more than 12i per cent the board has in mind that only through volume production can the Canadian farm implement industry survive, under the present level of costs and selling prices so that the price increase now authorized means that the companies must do their utmost to achieve a maximum volume of production. That I should add is exactly what is needed to meet the chronic shortages of farm implements which exist to-day. It will be of interest to recall also that on July 1, 1944, the exchange tax and all customs duties were removed from imported farm implements so that farmers are now assured that the Canadian price level must be fully competitive with other markets. I am further informed that retail farm implement prices in the North American continent are at least 25 per cent lower than in any other market in the world to-day.
To sum up, I wish to say that with the price adjustment now authorized and with the steps taken to give priority assistance in the securing of raw materials, such as steel, castings and component parts, I believe that the serious shortage in farm implements will begin to be remedied this year. I must warn, however, that with the best will in the world all shortages cannot be overcome immediately and that factors beyond our control, such as, for example, the recent strike in the steel industry in the United States, and the present coal strike, can seriously upset all forecasts or plans. It follows that strong inflationary influences are present in this field, both here and in the United States where about 50 per cent of our supplies of farm machinery and implements are obtained. For example, the United States farm implement industry during the months of January and February, 1946, showed a production decrease of, roughly,
20 per cent over the same months of 1945, or figured in dollars a total of some $110,000,000. Because of the dependence of the Canadian farm implement industry upon the United States for certain essential components, such a sharp decrease there inevitably affects production here.
The squeezed down price increase which has been allowed in the Canadian field of manufacture will, with the cooperation of the farm implement industry, ensure a maximum production in our own field of manufacture to the full extent that materials and labour are available, but there remains a very definite hazard that more serious price advances in import prices, over which we, of course, have no control, may yet be witnessed. *

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has just made a statement with respect to the announced policy of raising the price ceiling- on farm machinery by 12J per cent. He has sought to justify that policy on the grounds of increasing costs to the manufacturers and of the need for human food.
I want to commend the minister for making this statement, because it gives us some idea of the justification the government offers for this proposed increase. When the house adjourned on Friday evening we learned of the forthcoming announcement to be made through the press-and I am sure we are pleased to hear from the minister to-day. But I do not think I should let this opportunity pass without saying two or three things about the matter.
Speaking for those around me on this side, I think the government is going about the process of removing controls in the wrong order. Here is an increase in the price of farm machinery with no corresponding increase in the price of farm products. It is an increase in the price of farm machinery at the time that farmers are starting to seed their crops, and at a time when the world is short of food. As I say, I think the government's policy is to be criticized for the way in which the government is going about it, and for the timing of the announcement. The machinery which the farmers need to-day is already in the shops, and yet the prices to be paid for it are tomorrow's prices and not yesterday's. I welcome the minister's statement, but I am afraid we cannot support the policy or the reasons he has given for it.
It follows an announcement of a few days ago of an increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel, at which time there was no announcement that anything would be done to make possible an increase in the wages of steelworkers. I submit that the plans for the
Farm Implements

removal of these controls ought to be better correlated than they are, according to the evidence we have.

The hon. member wishes to avail himself of the privilege afforded by standing order 31 to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a matter which in his opinion is urgent. Before going any further I ryould call his attention to a ruling given by the Hon. Mr. Rhodes, then Speaker, on April 5, 1918, which wrill be found at page 744 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition:
There is one point mentioned by the hon. member to which I would reply, and more especially for the benefit of proper decorum in the house on the matter of urgency. Urgency, within the meaning of the rule, is not a question whether the matter proposed to be discussed is of urgent importance-
And I insist upon these words.
-it may be of infinitely urgent importance to those affected-the question is whether it is urgent within the meaning of rule 39: in other words, whether it is a matter of that urgency which would cause harm to the public interest if the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house were not able to permit the subject to be brought on early enough.
It is the duty of the Speaker to point out to the house that we have before us now routine proceedings and orders of the day and that preparations have already been made for the consideration of to-day's business. It is my duty to see that these orders of the day are followed. Hon. members, have been apprised since Friday last of the business
1" that would come on to-day and have prepared themselves accordingly. I realize that it is the privilege of every member to avail himself of standing order 31 and to move that

the business prepared for to-day shall be set aside to enable him to move the adjournment of the house. It is for the Speaker to decide whether the matter which it is proposed to discuss is of sufficient urgency and of sufficient public importance to warrant the suspension of the order of business. On this question the Speaker has not to decide "whether the matter proposed to be discussed is of urgent importance," but to decide whether it is urgent within the meaning of standing order 31. speechtext: Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 54, to amend the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, 1942.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942 -REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942 -REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: I expected that.

speechtext: We expected it, too.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942 -REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
We are in unanimous agreement. In 1942, parliament passed1 the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, to provide assurance to members of the armed forces of their right to reinstatement upon discharge, in the employment they were engaged in at the time of acceptance for service. The act provides that such reinstatement shall be on conditions not less favourable than if such persons had continued in the employer's employment without interruption.
In administering the act at earlier stages of the last war, a number of uncertainties arose on matters of interpretation and on the application of the act to circumstances which probably were not contemplated at the time the act was passed. It was, of course, important that reinstatement should not be held up on account of these uncertainties. Therefore

regulations under the authority of the War Measures Act were passed in January, 1945, which included not only matters of procedure under the act but also provisions designed to clear up the uncertainties relating to the interpretation and application of the Act. These regulations have now been in effect for some fifteen months and I am advised have been found suitable and effective to carry out the purposes of the act.
Employers andi labour organizations have extended the utmost cooperation in reinstatement of veterans and have shown much initiative in working out plans to this end in individual establishments. In consequence, the number of cases requiring the intervention of the officers of the Department of Labour ad^ ministering the act have been comparatively few to date. The purpose of the bill is to incorporate at this time the regulations approved by the governor in council under the War Measures Act as part of the provisions of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act and thus give statutory effect to them.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, a' moment ago I made a motion which was declared out of order, possibly on the technical ground raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that it had not been brought in at the proper stage of proceedings. If the motion is out of order I think that should be made clear on its merits, rather than on any technical grounds. I understand this is the proper time to bring it in. I would therefore move the motion again; and if on its merits it is out of order a ruling can be so made and it will be obeyed.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the government's policy as announced last Saturday of permitting an increase of 12J per cent in

Farm Implements

the ceiling price of farm implements without permitting a corresponding increase in the price of farm products, and thus imposing on the farmers extra production costs just at the time when they are preparing maximum production to meet the critical food situation.

subtopic: INCREASE IN RETAIL PRICE CEILINGS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
A few moments ago I had the opportunity to give to hon. members the 'practice followed in this house as far as these matters are concerned. Now, since there is some objection, and since the house is master of its own proceedings, I will put to the house the question whether or not the hon. gentleman shall have leave to proceed.
And leave having been given:

subtopic: INCREASE IN RETAIL PRICE CEILINGS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There is very little more I desire to say, Mr. Speaker, in addition to what I said a short time ago. Had the house permitted me to make that brief statement we would have let it go at that. I simply wish to point out that the best order was not followed in removing these controls, and that the timing was not well considered in this instance. At the very time the producers are starting to sow their crops they learn that farm machinery is going to cost them twelve and a half per cent more.
One other criticism is this. Last Friday evening we heard of a forthcoming announcement to raise farm machinery prices, which was carried in the newspapers on Saturday morning, and to-day we have the decision of the wartime prices and trade board explained by the minister. He brings it in at the opening of the house, with hon. members given no opportunity to debate it. I took what opportunity there was to say something against it; when I was denied the privilege of saying a word or two more, this motion had to be moved if others were to be allowed to speak.
I simply wish to say that the way these matters are handled

with decisions made outside the house, then explained here by a minister at a time when they are not debatable-it simply makes of this parliament with respect to these matters nothing more or less than a listening post.
I have said all I wish to say. Here is a measure increasing the cost of farm machinery without permitting an increase in the prices of farm products, just as two weeks ago another government decision was made which increased the price of steel by S5 a ton without at the same time making provision for some increase in the wages of steelworkers. That is my criticism. The policy is most unbalanced and inequitable. I could
take longer, but this is the protest I wished to make, and those are some of the points I had in mind.
Mr. M- J- COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar): I want to support the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) in his criticism of the procedure, though I know it is in conformity with the rules of the house. When an ahnouncement of this importance is made I do believe hon. members should be given an opportunity to debate it; and I am pleased indeed, Mr. Speaker, that you have afforded hon. members that opportunity, because of course I realize that it was quite possible for you to deny hon. members the right to discuss this matter under the usual procedure of this house.
May I say to the government through you, sir, that we in this party have been warm supporters of the idea that the government must have certain powers in order to exercise control to stabilize prices generally so that there shall be no runaway inflation, and we have supported that policy both in this house and in the country. But several things that have been done recently by the government have tended to increase the cost of producing agricultural products. Recently in western Canada we had increases in the cost of gasoline, fuels and so on. Now we have an increase of 12J per cent in the prices of agricultural implements. May I add, here that while I rise this afternoon to protest against this increase, we recognize that if the price ceilings are to be removed from one set of commodities, the prices of all other commodities will have to be adjusted as well. There must be no inconsistency in our attitude in that regard. Some of my hon. friends of the official opposition who have been urging the removal of price ceilings are now protesting against the removal of the price ceiling on agricultural implements. We are not in that position of inconsistency.
May I say this, while I am on my feet, that in 1938 this house established a committee, of which I was a member, which went into the question of the high prices of agricultural implements. We found at that time that in many respects the high prices which then existed on agricultural implements could not be justified. We made certain recommendations to the house and to the government with a view to lowering the prices of farm implements in the interests of agricultural producers. So far as I know, up to date at least none of the major recommendations of that committee has been adopted either by the government or by the companies.
Farm Implements

I wish to support very strongly the protests made against this increase. At a time when we are trying to maintain a certain measure of stabilization in our economy we have this increase in prices of farm implements. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has mentioned that we have also had an increase in the price of steel. Again I agree with him that this increase of S5 a ton in the price of steel was exactly the same increase as was made in the United States. But in the United States that $5 increase was granted on the condition that a certain increase should be made to the workers in the steel industry. In our country there has been no conference with the workers and no such condition. But the $5 increase has been handed out, and probably to some extent it is reflected in the announcement made to-day that the prices of agricultural implements are to be allowed to increase by 121 per cent. That is not the kind of policy we expect from the government, or that the people of this country expect from parliament. If we are to have stabilization, then let us have stabilization. If the farmers are to be compelled to accept stabilized prices for their products-prices well below American levels, as has been pointed out incidentally-then I say that other industries upon which farmers rely for their supplies should also be held at proper levels.
I can see no justification for this-either for the increase in the price of steel, or from my recollection of the results of the inquiry into the high prices of farm implements. We found then that the cost of distributing farm implements was excessive. We found that the costs shown as charged to farmers for service rendered by implement companies were excessive. Now we find ourselves faced with an increase which is indeed very serious. We know that tariff adjustments have been made in the interests of manufacturers; the' matter of diesel engines was discussed at the last session. In all these things it is indicated clearly that while workers are being held at certain wage levels, and farmers are being held at certain price levels, some of these large manufacturing concerns are to be allowed to increase their price levels. This house, every side of it-at least those of us who represent constituencies which are agricultural-should protest against the putting into effect of this kind of policy.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in protesting against this increase in the prices of farm machinery, which comes as the result

of an order made last Saturday by the wartime prices and trade board. I had intended to raise this question at the proper time, and to move the adjournment of the house as has already been done by the leader of the opposition.
I am pleased to note, sir, that you have been good enough to grant us this time to discuss a most important matter-because I do believe it is important. It is a matter which [DOT] should receive the earnest and full attention of every hon. member.
My reasons for preparing to ask for the adjournment were as follows. In the first place the order will have no less effect than to increase the cost of the production of farm products. The farmers will simply have to pay higher prices for their machinery. Everyone knows they have been paying too high prices already, owing to the protection afforded farm machinery manufacturing in Canada. The farmers in our country have certainly been at a great disadvantage owing to the high prices they have had to pay.
In the second place, in my judgment the increase in the prices of farm machinery threatens to defeat the all-out food production programme announced by the government just about a month ago. I feel certain, from the reaction of farmers already indicated, that this doubtless will cause widespread consternation among them. They certainly will not be ready to go forward willingly-as I am sure they were ready to go forward at the call of the Prime Minister in his food programme.
In my judgment the board's order intensifies the already serious handicap under which farmers have been operating for some time past, that of having their farm produce prices stabilized at levels lower than world price levels. It has put them at a terrific disadvantage as compared with the position enjoyed by farmers just across the line immediately to the south of us. Not only are our prices stabilized at levels lower than world price levels, but the border is closed to the export of cattle and live stock generally. This makes it difficult for our farmers to carry on in competition with their American neighbours. Unless remedial action is taken at once, this order of the wartime prices and trade board will have the effect of curtailing the production of agricultural goods at a time when every pound of foodstuffs is of the utmost importance in filling the world shortage, the great world need.
This is even more serious, coming as it does at a time when the spring work is about to begin. The farmers have already made up their budgets and plans for the year. It comes also at the end of six years of shortage

Farm Implements
of farm machinery, and at a time when farmers find it absolutely essential to increase their depleted stocks and to replace that which has been worn out.
The board's order imposes upon the Canadian farmers a burden of cost which they simply cannot 'bear, particularly so long as the level of taxation remains as it is in Canada, and so long as the farm commodity price stabilization policy continues in effect at present levels. In my judgment the board's order has precipitated a crisis in agriculture in this country. Therefore it does become a matter of grave urgency, and one to which the house should give its closest attention.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has said in his statement, it may be that some revision of prices should be made at this time. I am not fully convinced of that yet. I should like to have further figures to supplement the statement already made by the minister. However, I have always taken the position, in connection with the control of prices, that should it become necessary to revise, let us by all means consider the revision carefully. Let us do it along sane lines, and make certain that any increase in prices is justified. That is why I am certain that hon. members, and particularly farm members throughout Canada, are anxious to take part in this discussion to see to it that these price adjustments are justified. Should it be found that the increase of 12J per cent is justified then, to ease the minds of farmers, and to make certain that they will feel like continuing an all-out effort to relieve the food shortage throughout the world, I suggest that the government take into immediate consideration the absorption of those price increases by continuing the present prices'of farm machinery to farmers, the difference being made up by a subsidy gathered through taxation from all the people of Canada. That is the only justifiable way of handling the situation.
My colleagues and I strongly urge that this action be taken to set at rest the minds of the farmers, to let them understand that we are aware of their problems and that we are attempting to assist them in their all-out effort to produce food in large quantities sufficient to satisfy the need.
I am happy to join in this effort to understand the whole problem, and in the discussion of it. I do not wish to say more at this time.

I want to deal for a moment with the position of the machine companies. We remember that during the depression no substantial reduction was made in the price of farm machinery. There was a substantial reduction in the production of machinery, but not in the price. The reduced production arose out of the reduced demand because the farmers did not have the money to buy the machines. In 1937-38 the price of farm machinery went up 7-8 per cent, and the excuse given at that time was that owing to the lack of sales the overhead had increased and the price must be increased. One may well ask if there was any justification for an increase in price even at that time. I recall that the committee which was set up in 1937 found that the profits earned by the International Harvester company from 1926 to 1935 were 6-5 per cent. That,"at any rate in the later years, was a period of low production. Yet in spite of the fact that they earned a profit of 6-5 per cent up to 1935, they increased the price by 7-8 per cent in 1937. Incidentally this increase in price came just after the report of the farm implements committee, which was very critical of the high prices, was tabled in this house and concurred in-the increase showing an utter contempt on the part 'of machine companies apparently, for the opinions of this house. At that time an interesting report was given to the house on the operations of one of the large machine companies in this country. I hold in my hand a volume of Hansard of 1938 containing the report of a speech made by the chairman of the farm implements committee when moving, on March 11, concurrence in the report. This is what he had to say regarding the operations of the Massey-Harris company, as reported on pages 1238 and 1239:
We find that the Massey-Harris company does 60 per cent of its business outside of Canada. In 1891, when the Massey and Harris interests were merged, together with some other manufacturers, they had a capital of approximately $3,500,000. of which only $300,000 was put up in cash, the remainder being given in exchange for the assets of the constituent firms that were merged. In that period. 1891 to 1912, the capital remained at $3,500,000 leaving out of consideration for the moment another $1,000,000 that was put in in 1911. What do we find happening during that period? On a capitalization of $3,500,000 this company was able to pay cash dividends amounting to $11,212,349 and stock dividends of $8,500,000, or total dividends of $19,712,349; to create a rest account of $6,500.000; to set up a special contingency account of
$1,680,000 and to retain unallocated in surplus account $1,061,000, or a total of $28,959,349. That is a very substantial return, on a capital which amounted to $3,500,000 at the inception of the company and which remained at that figure until near the end of that period, when an additional $1,000,000 was put in. I am sure no one would say the prices this company charged its customers during that period were not sufficient to pay them a good rate of interest on the original investment, to give their stockholders sufficient in the way of dividends and still leave a very, very wide margin. Such is the situation with regard to that company, and broadly speaking it may be said to apply to many of the other companies, with perhaps a little less force.
That is from the speech made by the chairman of the committee which had been investigating these companies; I think therefore it bears a fair amount of weight.
I do not suppose there is any doubt that these companies have done pretty well for themselves during the war. It is not likely that they have been producing at a loss. In the earlier stages of the war I read reports in the Financial Post as to their profits, which at that time appeared to be very satisfactory. What is the situation to-day? Unquestionably the volume of business for the machine companies will be very heavy, and the greater the amount of their business the larger the reduction, of course, in their overhead cost. It was brought out in the committee investigation in 1937 that costs of collection and losses incurred through bad debts were quite heavy, representing in the neighbourhood of five per cent. As I understand it, that loss will be entirely eliminated, because as a result of certain legislation passed in this house farmers will be able to pay cash for their machines, as they can go to the banks and borrow the money. Machinery companies will not be selling their machinery on time, so losses such as they suffered in the past as a result of bad debts and heavy collection fees will be wholly eliminated. This should make it possible for the companies to reduce their costs quite considerably. If, however, as the leader of this group pointed out, it should be found that the companies must be allowed to increase their prices in order to carry on, we shall have to do one of two things; either remove the ceiling on the price of agricultural products so Ihat the farmers will not be obliged to sell at a loss, or have the additional cost absorbed by the people as a whole instead of by the farmers alone, as we did during the war. We imported goods which cost more than the price at which they were sold under the price ceiling, and the government subsidized those firms so that they could sell at a discounted price in this country without losing money. If the govern-
Farm Implements

ment feels that the machine companies must increase their prices by 12J per cent in order to avoid loss, let the government subsidize them to that extent and let the cost be borne by the people of Canada instead of by the farmers alone.
This government has unfortunately contracted the habit of subsidizing the people of this country and the people of the world in respect of agricultural produce and putting the full cost of the subsidy on the farmer alone instead of distributing it among all the people. We have a good instance of that practice in that we are selling wheat to Europe at $1.55 a bushel. Our party do not object to that for a minute, but in view of the fact that the world price is around $1.98-that is the selling price in Chicago-if we are to sell to Britain at $1.55 the farmers should not have to absorb that loss alone; it should be absorbed by the people as a whole. Indeed, the farmers are not even receiving $1.55; they are receiving $1.25, though of course they hope that at some future date the participation certificates will make up the difference.
I should like again to emphasize that we feel the government should do one of two things. If the government is going to take price ceilings off goods which form part of the cost of farm production, it should take the ceiiing off agricultural products. You cannot continually increase the cost of the implements of production while keeping a ceiling on the price of the articles produced. If, on the other hand, the government is not prepared to do that, it should, as the leader of this group has pointed out, allow a discount on the price of machinery and subsidize the machine companies to that extent.

Mr. PATRICK H. ASHBY (Edmonton East): Agriculture is big business. Ii do not know who designed these chairs, Mr. Speaker. Sometimes I wonder if those who erected and furnished these buildings had any imagination. Walking down these corridors I get a smell from the match factory across the river, and I say to myself, "What a Hull of a smell 1" I sometimes wonder what imagination, sir, the individual had who gave you the title of Mr. Speaker; for I notice that you do the least speaking in the house, although I must admit you say more when you do not get on your feet than many hon. members do who speak from the floor. I do not think I can do better than to read from Hansard of December 14 last at page 3491. I may be criticized for agreeing with this, but I believe it was the statement of a great man:
A member of parliament represents the people of the nation at large-all classes.
That statement was made by the Prime Minister, and I raise my hat to him for those words. If hon. members will appreciate the truth of what he said on that occasion they will realize we are not here to represent the farm machinery companies. We are here to represent the farmers as well-all classes. I do not see how any human being could utter greater words than those, and if the individual members of the Liberal' party realize their significance, we would go far. In fact, I honestly believe that we in Canada would accomplish a great deal, if the Prime Minister meant what he said, and I am taking it for granted that he did. I am not listening to what other people tell me. He says that we are here to represent all the people, all classes, and I can assure the house that if we get behind the spirit indicated by those
words and fight to represent the people of Canada, all the people, we shall go far. Indeed,
I believe we can show the world that we in this great dominion can lead mankind out of dhaos and into a period of prosperity and happiness such as has never been known before in human history.
The Prime Minister told my wife and me that he was seventy-two years of age.
I believe he has an opportunity to leave his name with us for generations to come as a great man; for he has the opportunity to-day to see that all the people of Canada are represented here. I am not a Liberal. I do not believe in liberalism, conservatism, socialism, communism or any other "ism". I believe in results, and I will join with any individual or group df individuals-I think I can speak for this group when I say this- who will truly represent the will of the people. We will join with any party who will represent the will of the people, and we will give that party our whole-hearted support.
Let me read some more. The Prime Minister said:	[DOT]
I do not think it is desirable . . . that any man should come here to represent any organization except his own constituency. I do not care whether it is a trade union organization or any other organization, a man ought to be here to represent the general interests of his constituents.
As things are to-day, with this 12i per cent increase, there is only one way that it can be paid and that is by the farmer, through a . lowering of his standard of living. And the farmer, of all people in Canada, is the one who has suffered most during this war. I know that, because I was farming during the war, and so were my wife and children and the wives and children of other farmers throughout Canada. They toiled and sweated, the majority of them without pay or remuneration of any kind. During the war our neighbour's boys were taken out of school to work on a farm, as was many a son, and those boys worked not for a mere eight hours a day but for ten and sixteen hours a day. I remember one night, when it started to rain those boys could not go to bed but had to continue working up until midnight in order to protect their crops and they were working with old worn-out machinery. Three of these boys did not want to bother their mother, who was already too tired from the day's work. They were too tired even to go and wash. They went to sleep in a shack which was filled with the fumes of a motor used for charging batteries, and the next morning the mother found her sons there, cold and dead. This is just an indication of the sacrifices that were made by farm boys, farm


women and men during the war. Those who are trying to carry on are now being asked to pay, and pay in hard-earned money, to replace their worn-out machinery.
What results do we desire? We want to live here in Canada, and we can live. The method that we are now using in dealing with this problem is not the only one. There are alternative methods, and I can assure you, sir, that we can reward the farm machinery companies with a 12) per cent increase, enabling them to continue the service they are rendering to the workers in the factories and at the same time sell the machinery for less than 12) per cent higher. We can cut the price twenty-five per cent lower than pre-war prices and sell to the farmers without loss to ^nyone. It is merely a matter of method. There are a dozen methods, devised and known, some good, some bad, which will enable us to do that. What is more, we can cut the price of farm produce to the consumer; for the ultimate object we have in producing is to enable the consumer to enjoy the fruits of the production. Just as we produced war materials to the tune of billions of dollars, shipped them overseas and delivered them to the enemy, absolutely free, so we can produce farm machinery and give it free to the farmers without loss to anyone. It is merely a little different method; that is all.
We can double the production of all farm [DOT] produce at any time agriculture is free to go ahead. The machinery companies will produce the necessary machinery; I have no doubt whatever of that. They are the experts, and if they are given the opportunity to do so, they can produce machinery which will enable one farmer to produce as much as a hundred farmers did before. I can guarantee to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that if farmers are given their freedom to produce, we can do more than double production; we can produce ten pounds of butter and ten quarts of milk for every pound of butter and quart of milk produced before, without increasing the number of live stock on our farms, without increasing the acreage in production, and at no additional cost to the consumer. In fact we shall be able to sell even cheaper. It is merely a matter of method. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is wrong to force the farmer to pay more for his farm machinery. He can be given the finest machinery and pay less for it than he is paying now.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCO IS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, in this case it is quite evident that the ruling was decided upon after the representations were made by the

manufacturers of implements. I doubt very much whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) sought the advice of the farmers or any farmers' organization. I know at that time a real attempt was made to prove that the prices of farm implements were too high, but I was never convinced of this. I thought the companies made out a very good case to show that their profits were fairly reasonable, and1 that they could not continue to produce if prices were reduced to any considerable extent. It is true that we had a recent increase of four cents in the price of butter and 82 in the price of hogs, but that does not begin to establish a balanced economy in this country as far as the farmer is concerned.
To a very great extent the farmer bore the brunt of increased costs of production during the war. Lately he has been getting a lower price for his wheat than is being paid in the United States. Now we are told that there is to be an increase in the cost of his implements of production. I wonder if this twelve and a half per cent increase will guarantee that the farmer will get sufficient implements with which to carry on. During the war the farmer was not able to buy the implements he required, and to day many of his machines are obsolete. Labour is also very scarce. In my own riding an investigation was made which showed that in this dairy county there was an average of only twelve men to every thousand acres. The farmer needs new implements, and unless he can get the money with which to buy them he will not be in a position to carry on. During the war the farmer was loyal enough to work twelve or fifteen hours a day in order to produce foodstuffs, but now the war is over he is inclined to sit back and take things a little more easily. That I think is what he intends to do, unless he is given a better deal.
I do not intend to say anything further, but I do believe that if this increase in the farmers' cost of production has been found necessary, there should have been corresponding increases in the prices of the things the farmers produce.

It seems to me this twelve and a half per cent represents a very large increase in the prices of farm machinery. We all know that such machinery is very scarce, and we all know that during the war farmers worked with worn out machines. We also know that as a result we must have mass production, for there must be a tremendous need for farm equipment throughout the country, which also should mean mass sales. As some one has pointed out, this in itself should mean that the cost of farm machinery ought not to rise to any great extent. I mentioned that farmers have had to carry on with worn out machinery. We all know that if there is a farm auction anywhere in the district the farmers flock to it by the hundreds in order to purchase whatever machinery may be available.
My main reason for rising, Mr. Speaker, was to point out to the minister that one particular class will be greatly affected by this increase in price. I refer to the soldier settler, the man who has just returned after five years of service overseas; the man who is being encouraged .by the Department of Veterans Affairs and by the government in general to take up farming. He is beginning from scratch, as it were. As the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) knows, we in the veterans committee are trying to make things as easy as possible for these soldier settlers, and I fear this is going to be a direct slap at these men, who have planned on buying their machinery at current' prices. Now they will find they must pay twelve and a half per cent more, which I am sure will be a great disappointment to them. I hope that some further arrangements may be made *which will be equitable as far as the veterans are concerned.
I might also point out to the minister, as other hon. members have mentioned, that here in Canada we are trying to stem the flow from the farms to the cities. Our cities and towns are greatly overcrowded; we have thousands of men and women in them without homes, while in the country we have hundreds of homes without people living in them. I think everything possible should be done to encourage the trek not from the country to the cities but back from the cities and towns to the country. Otherwise I fear we are going to have a very unbalanced

I do not think I have anything further to say. As I said before, I was not in the house when the minister made his explanation. We should encourage our farmers. They are given four cents per pound increase in the price of butter, but the farmers in my constituency-and in that constituency they are chiefly dairy farmers-do not consider that increase was enough. They have tried to produce butter during the war at ceiling prices, with the result that thousands of them went out of butter production and sold their raw milk, or engaged in the production of cheese.
These matters should be carefully considered. I hope it has been well considered, and that it will not react unfavourably-as it seems it might-to the farmers of this country.

My observations, therefore, will be particularly directed toward the point of view of workers' wages. Before dealing with that, may I say that I believe it will be only a matter of
minutes before some member of the government will rise in his place, look across at this side and say: What are you complaining about? You have been advocating the removal of price ceilings from many products
I would therefore remind the government at the outset that foremost in our programme for raising ceilings is the raising of the ceiling on workers' wages, and, second, raising the ceiling on the price of farm products. Both of these policies are at complete loggerheads with the present policy of the government. Therefore the government must not be surprised if they find the Progressive Conservative party advocating that the present policy be given further thought. I believe the minister should tell us whether there is a wage increase for the workers in the farm machinery manufacturing companies which is to be discovered, perhaps, by the same means that the steel workers discoverd theirs, or whether this is a direct advance in price and the manufacturer will get the complete benefit. The minister should also tell us whether the wartime prices and trade board have any machinery of coordination with the national labour board, because it seems to me that the government is out of step with itself all the time; that these two boards do not coordinate their work, and that as a result, when the price of a commodity increases the workers must separately seek their share of the price increase.
But my real reason in rising, Mr. Speaker, is to deal with this as a fundamental question and not as one purely of the wages of labour or of an increase of price. In my opinion, there are three possible reasons for this price increase. It may be the result of pressure group action upon the government; it may be, as the minister says, to stimulate full production; or it may be to meet a corresponding rise in prices and costs in the United States. I do not believe that the government would submit to a pressure group at this time; at least I will give them credit for that. I do not think the minister can be convinced that a 124 per cent increase of the selling price of farm machinery will result in full production or, indeed, increase it. I submit that this price rise is probably caused by the inflation of United States economy which is having its effect on us at the present time and which is being felt all across Canada. The position of this industry is only one instance of the ways in which our country is being influenced by United States prices of accessories and finished parts. The government are not tackling this problem from its fundamental cause; when they permit a rise in the selling price of one group of articles

Farm Implements

they are not going to the root of the matter. The root of the matter is that our Canadian economy is not so organized that it can protect itself against the economy of the United States of America. Fundamentally, it cannot protect itself because the United States is suffering inflation at the present time, and in my opinion this is only a beginning of its effect on Canada. We are going to meet this problem in connection with many other lines of goods especially in cases where we find ourselves dependent on the United States for either fully manufactured products, semifinished products, or articles which are assembled in this country. Instead of putting the wartime prices and trade board to work figure out various price increases, we should put them to work to figure out ways to protect our Canadian economy from these dangers of inflation; and it should be the job of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) to see that all these products which we have to import, to assemble and to use in the manufacture of this machinery should begin to be produced by ourselves here and now. Then the minister will be protected, and he will not have price rises forced upon him by inflation south of our border.
I rise simply to submit these two points to the house: that no mention has been made of wage increases; that no mention has been made of the fact that the Massey-Harris Company of Canada, which was on war work, has been unable to increase its wages, and actually, at a time of rising prices, workers are receiving less for their money than they were during the war. The minister should also try to find ways of protecting the Canadian economy from the dangers of inflation in the United States.

I am not in favour of that course of action, because I do not believe that in a democratic country we should be placed in a position where we have to do that sort of thing, and particularly so at this time, when food is so greatly needed in Europe.
In the speech from the throne we find this:
Every encouragement is being given to increasing production.

On the night of March 17 the nine-point programme was announced. Then on March 18 there was an increase of two cents a gallon in the price of motor fuels. I believe I need not say much more, However, again on behalf of the farmers of Canada I demand a percentage of the national income which will compensate them for their contribution, an amount of that national income to which we are entitled.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make only a few brief remarks, because even now I am fairly well exhausted, having risen thirteen times in an effort to take part in this debate.
May I express my disappointment at this increase in the price of agricultural implements, and at the manner in which this has been done. If labour requires an increase in wages, it has to submit proposals and figures which are made known to the public generally. Everything is done in the open. The press carries the facts concerning arbitration or conciliation boards, and nothing can be hidden. If the farmers want an increase in commodity prices they must come out in the open, give their evidence publicly and attempt to prove that they are entitled to increases in their prices, because of increased) production costs. In the present instance, however, through the method of handling price increases 63260-561
by the wartime prices and trade board the increase is presented to us as a fait accompli.
I fully appreciate the difficulty facing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and I believe persons who discuss matters of this type should be constructive in their criticism. It is very easy to make general statements or offhand remarks. As I said in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, I believe we are entering into another phase of capitalism. We are developing in Canada a form of state capitalism, and if we are to negotiate the years ahead safely we shall have to use new techniques and develop new methods. This we must do, if we wish to prevent the vicious circle of prices, wages, and inflation.
I suggest that the Minister of Finance and the government consider the possibility of arriving at these decisions in a more democratic way. When it comes to a consideration of prices and wages I suggest that the government, the Department of Labour, the wartime prices and trade board and the ministers involved should call in for consultation representatives of labour, representatives from the farming community and representatives from industry.
I see no way of avoiding economic chaos unless we develop some technique of that type. Then, if we are to reestablish confidence in the country and in one another there must be frankness, and a placing of all the facts on the table. In this way I am sure decisions acceptable to the country at large and receiving its support can be arrived at. The government would still have-and must have- the responsibility for governing the country, but I am sure if we are to negotiate safely the years lying immediately ahead we must develop a technique of that type.

The minister knows, but I do not know. I mean that the ordinary rank and file member does not know, but just the men at the top. That is one of the things to which I object. Take the position of organized workers asking for an increase in wages. Generally they first have to take a strike vote. This procedure is to show that they mean business, that if something is not done they will go on strike. But that is a procedure which they have to go through. Then they have to make an application to the regional war labour board.. On that board will sit the representatives of employers, representatives of the workers, and a supposedly neutral or impartial chairman or representative of the government. Then that board makes a finding. But that is not the end of it. After that finding is made it must be reported to the national war labour board. Either side, of course, may appeal to the national war labour board against the finding. There again you have the same thing; there will be representatives of labour, representatives of employers, and a representative of the government. But when the employers come for an increase in prices they go into a closed room. There is no representative of labour there. There is no representative of the consumer there. There is
nobody there except the officers of the wartime prices and trade board and the people who are asking for the increase. We have one law and one procedure for the workers; we have another law and another procedure for business. And business during the entire war controlled the whole of our economy, and have come out of the war much better than they were when they went into it.
One case which has been brought to my attention is that of the Guelph Stove company, owned exclusively, I believe, by the T. Eaton company. The employees of this company asked for a raise in the basic wage from fifty cents to fifty-five cents. They went to the regional war labour board of Ontario, which granted the increase. The company appealed to the national war labour board. The national war labour board wiped out the increase granted by the regional board; it allowed the employees a few small concessions, something on overtime and .perhaps holidays with pay, but denied them the basic increase which had been granted by the regional board. Why do manufacturers and business men, when they want an increase in price, not have to go through the same procedure, a procedure at which the public and labour are represented? If it is proper that employers shall have a voice in decisions on wages, I maintain it is proper that the workers should have a voice when it is a question of prices, because ultimately labour has to pay its share of the increased prices. The case I mentioned, that of the Guelph Stove company, is the first decision, I think, made by the national war labour board since P.C.9384 was amended to make it easier to get an increase in wages. That just shows how "easy" it has been made. I suggest that if we are to have a reasonable, rational, fair deal in this matter of wages and prices, before any increase of either is granted, both applications should go through the same process.
I believe it was the hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Senn) who, in speaking this afternoon, said that in the farm implements investigation during the session of 1937 the committee was not sure whether prices of farm implements were too high or not. I have before me the journals of the house for that session. I wush to quote from page 500, a part of the lengthy report which was made by the committee of the house. prices. Particularly do I hold that view in a time of crisis. In fact, not so long ago I voted for the extension of such powers to be exercised by the present government. Nor do I think, as was suggested by an hon. member in this debate, that such procedure necessarily means the establishment of a bureaucracy because, as I understand this situation, no board in Canada has absolute authority to do anything, 'but the minister and the government must accept responsibility for the statement which was made to-day by the minister. That responsibility rests with this government and with this parliament. The same hon. gentleman said that the increase proposed was negotiated by the wartime prices and trade board, and he branded that body as a bureaucracy. It may be a bureaucracy, but I would rather submit to the findings of that board than to the bureaucracy of monopoly capital Which, without any board, would be raising prices without any question and without this parliament even having a chance to discuss the matter. It would be very interesting for this house to know whether the trades board gave the advice to the government in this matter or whether the government gave the advice to the trades board. I do not believe the board initiated this increase in prices, and when the minister speaks I hope he will prove my point by taking full responsibility for the statement he made, as I believe he will.
Nevertheless I was amazed at the statement itself, indicating an increase of 12J per cent in the price of farm machinery, and that this was done without those directly affected being given an opportunity to be heard, either by the board or by the government, or by both. It means, of course, an increase in the production costs of the farmers, without, as has been pointed out by nearly all the speakers preceding me, a corresponding increase in farmers' incomes. Similar increases have already been granted to other companies, without any corresponding increase in the wages of those employed in the plants privileged to raise their prices. So that I desire to protest against this increase. I protest against the principle; I protest against the method by which it was put into effect; I protest against the result it will bring, both to farmers and wage-earners.
For the past few years, during war time we have had what I might call stabilized prices. I suggest that it is unwise to alter any price in a stabilized system unless there is a complete revision touching all industries and all wage scales affected. It is not possible to alter the price of one commodity without adversely affecting all other indus-

tries and all other individuals. To do so, therefore, means that we are entering the vicious circle of inflation.
For instance, we had first of all an increase in the price of steel. It follows naturally that industries requiring steel in their production will seek to have an increase in their prices. Then it will follow that working people will ask for corresponding increases in wages; farmers will ask for corresponding increases in their income. When that is done the steel companies will ask for a greater increase to offset the increased costs brought about through increased wages and increased farm incomes, thereby effecting a complete circle. So that the dog of inflation will chase its own tail around the circle of our national economy, but never get a chance to catch it.
If there is to be any alteration in prices, then it should begin with workers and farmers, because they are at the lower end of the system. Their incomes are now and in the past have been relatively much less than those of the manufacturing fraternity. Manufacturers had much the best of it during the war. They made greater profits in that time, in spite of the profits tax, than they did in peace time. They vastly increased their reserves; they increased their capital assets and they decreased their corporation debts. In fact, profits in the war-time period took the form of increased assets and increased reserves. Still they are not satisfied.
In the second place, I am opposed to this increase because of the method by which it has been achieved. It has already been pointed out that there was no real inquiry. If there was, then it was all one-sided. I believe the minister indicated that the evidence warranted the action taken. But the evidence is not all in; it was one-sided. The evidence of agriculture and that of the workers was not there. I believe one hon. member emphasized the fact that when an increase in the tariff was to be made, the tariff board gave notice of an application. Then those who were interested were permitted to appear and to say why such increase should not be effected. In this instance, however, there was no such inquiry. Therefore I am opposed to a method which fails to give an opportunity to the industries directly affected to bring their position to the attention of the board, to point out how they would be affected by the proposed change.
Then I am opposed to the results. One hon. member has said he was out for results, and cared nothing about methods. Well, this is a result. But I submit that anyone who is out for a result cannot afford to ignore the only method by which a desired result can be

obtained. I am opposed to this result. The minister may say I am wrong in this, but I still await a refutation of what I say, namely that a 12J per cent increase in the price of farm rqachinery will certainly not reduce farmers' costs of production. If the minister can show how that is possible, I shall be greatly in his debt. Not only will it not reduce the cost of farm production, but I insist that if there is an increase in the price of farm machinery it must of necessity increase the cost of farm production.
As an hon. member to my right pointed out a few minutes ago, all our returned soldiers who intend to go farming must buy all their machinery. They have none. For that machinery they must pay the extra 12J per cent. Without doubt, those seem to be the facts in the case.
For some time there has been what I would call a systematic campaign put on by big business to influence the government, if possible-and probably the board-and to prepare . the public mind for acquiescence in a desired rise in prices. They have carried on this campaign to the extent of discouraging, as far as possible, the continuation of price controls by the administration. In this connection, let me mention some of the headlines which have appeared in the Financial Post, and then I would ask hon. members to draw their own conclusions as to what would follow from them. One says this, "Say growing goods famine is caused by price ceiling"-not caused by a shortage of material; not caused by a shortage of labour, but caused by the price ceiling.
Another heading states: "Output of essential goods slow as ceiling 'bonus' luxuries".
And another: "See black market booming if price controls maintained".
Those are headlines which suggest the campaign of industry and of big business to remove from the government all controls whatsoever.
I conclude by asking the minister what the facts are. He has said that the evidence was sufficient to justify the action taken, which was announced this afternoon. But, as I have said, only half of that evidence was heard. What are the facts? Will the minister put on record the actual financial position of the companies which have been permitted to raise their prices? Industries claiming the right to raise prices should be able to make public the facts showing the financial position warranting the increases demanded. If the minister can show such facts I am sure the house will receive his statement with a great deal , more grace than it can accept the position as it now stands.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those who have already spoken in protest against the 12) per cent increase in the cost of farm machinery.	*
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) said that he would like to see the statement or figures of the machine companies showing their present position. I agree with him, and I should like to see alongside those figures the income of our farmers from 1929 to 1939 and on up to the present time. I am sure that if the incomes of these two groups were to be compared we would find that it is the farmer that needs subsidizing and not the machine companies: It is my view that the government should not allow, should not even think of making this gift to the machine companies at the expense of the farmers, but if the minister still desires to make a gift to the machine companies he should look for another source of revenue from which to do so. It has been pointed out on many occasions by members of this group as well as by other groups in the house that the farmers of this country have been worse off than any other group of our citizens.
Surely after what our farmers had gone through during the depression years we should give them an opportunity now to get on their feet. During the past six years of war the farmers had to struggle along with a shortage of labour; they had to repair their old machinery, and now they are all in the market for new machinery. This is the time apparently when a number of the gentlemen in the farm machine business got together and thought that now is a good time to clean up on the farmers, to skin them alive. If members of this house representing agricultural constituencies do not stop this price increase they will have failed the farmers of this nation. If this is the type of new order* that was promised to our agriculturists during the war, who can tell what will happen to them five years from now? I protest as strongly as I can against any increase in the cost of farm machinery I feel that this is the time to be demanding a reduction in the price of farm machinery-not an increase.
I also wish to join with other hon. members in protesting against the method of arriving at this decision. I am going to be frank and say that this is the backdoor method. Why did the government not bring in a measure, place it openly before the representatives of the people in the House of Commons and let the people's representatives
Farm Implements

debate it? Then ii could have been sent to a committee of the house,, where witnesses could have been called so that we could have ascertained exactly what the situation was and in the light of the facts adduced arrive at the' proper decision. As it is, we are permitting a board to make a decision of this importance, to decide an issue which affects about thirty per cent of our total population. It is about time that we learned that the farmers of this nation are not going to keep on taking it on the chin as they have had to do in the past. It is about time they were consulted'. But I understand that the minister consulted no farm organizations, nor did he consult the members of parliament. Not a single farm organization was consulted, although this is a measure that directly affects agriculture. It seems to me that this is not the proper way of handling this problem.
As the leader of this group, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), has pointed out, should conditions warrant an increase in farm machinery it would then be up to the government to find ways and means of subsidizing the increased costs. Surely the farmer should not be expected to bear the whole burden.
Agriculture in this country, as we all know, is a basic industry. If agriculture prospers, Canada prospers. Should agriculture suffer, Canada will suffer. I for one would never like to see agriculture go back to the position in which it found itself between 1929 and 1939.
There has been a campaign carried on in the press and I have heard a number of speakers over the radio stating that Canada should get as many young Canadians as possible to go into agriculture. It is a back-to-the-land campaign. But if the government begins by increasing the price of farm machinery by 12J per cent it will simply be turning the boys away from the farms. If the government wants to deplete our rural population, this is the best way to do so. It would be a healthy sign if more of our young men were interested in agriculture. But when you put agriculture in the position where farmers have to pay more for their implements, and levy additional costs( you cannot blame the young men for going into the cities.
One further thought. If the government intends to discredit private enterprise, this is the best way of doing so; and if the government continues to pursue this course it will do just that, discredit private enterprise.
For the past number of years pur farmers have fed approximately 16,000,000 people. That is no small achievement, and surely this price increase is no small issue to be lightly brushed aside or decided by a board.

We should review farm income over the past fifteen or twenty years and at the same time review the earnings of the machine companies, so that we can arrive at a satisfactory comparison whether it is the machine companies or the farmers that need to be subsidized. Let us not forget that the farmers have carried on their farming operations during the war with old machinery, and that they are now all in the market to buy new farm implements. This decision of the board is a blow at agriculture which will bring no credit to this government. I am not so much concerned about who is going to clean up on this price increase. I want to see agriculture in Canada placed on a sound basis so that our farmers will get their share of the national income and so that their children will be able to attend schools and live like human beings, instead of being driven from place to place by the mortgage companies. If our farmers have to buy the machinery they need at increased prices and have to go into debt, then when prices of agricultural products fall it will be only another few years before the mortgage and trust companies will again be racing after our farmers up and down the country trying to collect.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that if the representatives of western Canada and the representatives of central Canada and of eastern Canada as well permit this increase to go through they will be failing their constituents; they will be failing our basic industry, and failing our nation at a time when the world is demanding greater production than ever before. At a time, when millions of human beings are starving in Europe, this is the action which the government takes without even giving it much thought.

country. Farms containing the very best of agricultural land are lying idle, for the simple reason that farmers cannot afford to work them. This is particularly evident in my own constituency. If this added burden of increased prices of machinery is put on the farmers, I am sure it will result in a further decrease of production instead of the increase which is so much desired.
