speechtext:
We are opposed to granting this increase in the price of farm machinery. The fact that it adds to the cost of production to the farmer upsets a great deal of the faith which the Canadian people have had in the government's policy of price control to prevent inflation. The minister, or the cabinet, or whoever advised this step have taken the wrong course, because they set ceilings on prices of farm products when the old prices on machinery were in operation, and now that the cost of production is increased to the farmer, the same ceilings remain on farm products. In all fairness to those concerned in the big business of raising food when the world needs it as it does today, this should be accompanied by an announcement on the part of the government that they are permitting an increase in the selling price of farm produce. This measure takes all the security out of agriculture, and without security people will not go into agriculture.
Further, I think the announcement was ill-timed from the point of view of the thousands of young men whom this government is trying to entice back on the land as they return from the war. Hundreds of thousands of young men wishing to take up agriculture as their life pursuit will say, "What security is there in this? What is the use of my undertaking a twenty or a ten-year agreement to pay back borrowed money if overnight it is to be announced that machinery prices will go up 12i per cent? To-morrow the price may go up another 15 per cent." They will begin to ask, "Where do we fit into this thing?"
Farm Implements

The farmer is commencing to wake up to the fact that what has been wrong with him in the past is that, whenever he went to town to buy anything-and in these days he must buy in order to operate-those who had commodities for sale always told him exactly what he must pay; he had to pay it or he went without; because he had to have it he had to pay what was charged, and he accepted the idea -that those who were selling should name the price. It is a funny thing, however, that when the farmer took his produce into town to sell it, instead of being able to say what price he should get, he usually had to go around and say, "Please, mister, what price will you pay me?" Until you put a floor under farm prices there can be no security, and there ought to be a guarantee against such increase of production cost as this, or some guarantee of the actual cost of farm machinery, so that the farmer will know over a period of years what his costs will be in this line. What assurance has he that in another three months the price will not again be increased with the government's consent?
The greatest harm which will be done is the loss of faith on the part of the people who are doing the work, and, after all, the people who toil are the people who produce the wealth from the land. Without the production of the men and women in the factory, without the production of the men, women and children on the farms we cannot have any wealth in this country; that is, any real wealth-the food and clothing and the shelter that man requires.
The other circumstance that makes the situation particularly serious is that the great-' est need of the world to-day is food. This government has so stated. It is recognized by all, and UNRRA and the united nations organization are emphasizing it. But this policy goes to the very root of production, which is falling off badly. I have here the figures for creamery butter and cheese production. If we take 1946, in January, creamery butter fell off 15'6 per cent and cheese, 27-8 per cent; in February, 1946, there was a drop of 18-3 per cent in creamery butter and 26-5 per cent in cheese. This is in comparison with the same months of 1945, and that has con-fallen off 19-6 per cent as compared with last year, and cheese, 35-5 per cent.
In these provinces we have the hay and the necessary materials, but the people are not producing. What is the trouble? There are a good many causes. It is time the government realized that the production of farm commodities is not an eight hour day job. If you are raising cattle or milking cows your job

starts early in the morning. A good many people are in the bams working at five o'clock in the morning and they work until eight o'clock at night. And it is not a five-day week that they put in, but a seven-day week, 365 days in the year, without any holidays and often without any pay. The government tells us that we are to have another cut in butter rations when we should be producing more than ever before. There are more men to go into production. The boys are returning from overseas. But they are not going on the farms. Why? We find the answer in just such legislation as this.
I wish to criticize the government also on its farm machinery policy in this regard, that they do not put any ceiling on the sale of secondhand machinery by agents. Recently in, my own city some ten thousand farmers came from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta to the city of Yorkton because an enterprising agent there had advertised that he had some sixty-nine reconditioned tractors for sale, and according to the press reports the bids ranged from $200 to $1,000 over and above prices of new tractors. So serious is the need for machinery. Without the labour, men must have the necessary machinery to save them toir, and the machinery companies cannot provide what is required. The farmers need these things, and to permit a 12^ per cent increase is bad enough, but to compel the farmers to get their machinery at 100 per cent increase is something that should not be tolerated. Ceilings are put on secondhand cars; why not on this machinery?
This is the last straw on the camel's back. Many things have been gradually added to the farmers' burden since the end of the war, one thing after another. There is the difficulty in getting labour and the increase in the wages the farmer has to pay. His returns are so small, and he has to pay income tax. I am glad the Minister of National Revenue is in his place. I have seen farmers go out of production in the west overnight in recent months when they found out the manner in which their income tax is to be collected.
A farmer I know came to me in December and said, "Is this what you call justice in this country? I operated this farm in 1942 and by the government regulations I was not permitted to sell my grain because there were quotas on it. My cash operations for 1942, owing to the fact that I could not sell my products, was $150 of a loss and my bins were full of grain. The year 1943 came along and the quotas were lifted slightly so that I sold part of the 1942 crop and part of the

Farm Implements
1943	crop. I had to build more bins to keep the stuff, and I was not allowed to sell it in view of government regulations. The result was that once again my bins were full. The year 1944 came along; we had a big crop and the government told us to sell grain and stock and cattle because this was necessary to feed the armies." Well, the farmers -went and sold stuff. These people have never known what it was to pay income tax because so many years of their lives have been spent in making losses. They would make $130 cash income for a year's work.
The farmers do not understand the intricacies and the complicated forms of income tax, and as to knowing what an accrual basis is, well, they do not know anything about it. One day this farmer whose case I am stating was ordered to appear and report on his income tax. The third reason is that I do not agree with the announcement that there should be an increase in the price of farm machinery; not that I do not think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) can justify his position by quoting figures to show that it is necessary to raise the price of farm machinery. I believe that he can. All through the years the price of farm machinery has been increased so substantially that it is not necessary now to increase it again. Before we can pay more for farm machinery it will be necessary to raise the price of farm produce an equal amount. The price of farm produce has been far too low for far too long. During the war years farmers generally carried on because we were at war. No one in this country will contend that they did not do a good job. A census taken in our community in the county of Huron showed that during those years the average age of farmers was fifty-six years. That will give the house some idea of the age of some of the farmers who were trying to farm. Many men seventy years of age and over were trying to run a 100 acre farm. These men carried on all through the war years because we were at war, not because they were able to do it. They now find their health impaired and they cannot carry on any longer. They have tried to get help but, because farming is not attractive, they could not get help. One has only to look at the 
number of returned men who have applied for farms to undertake farming to understand. It is true we have had some make application, but they do not amount to a large percentage of the boys who came back and who want to start farming. Many of these boys saved a couple of thousand dollars. They would rather put it into a wartime house costing S6.000 and depend on their monthly pay check to pay the remainder, than put it in a farm. I should like to suggest that the boys who are putting all their savings in wartime housing and are depending on industry to pay the remainder will, in seventy-five per cent of the cases, lose every dollar they have. These boys could take the money they have saved and go to the country, and while prices are not as good as some think they should be, they would at least save that portion of the money they tried to save during the war years.
Labour is demanding more money; the machinery companies are demanding more money and many other people are demanding more money. I should like to know what good money will be if we reach the stage where we cannot buy food. Take the devastated countries of Europe where they are starving. Money is not of any value when you cannot buy anything to eat with it. That is what we shall be faced with here. In almost every farming community in Canada we find house after house and farm after farm vacant. There are at least two or three in every mile and a quarter. Why? Simply because farming is not attractive enough to bring people to the farms. Many farms were made vacant during the first years of the war. People left these farms to go into industry, munition plants and the like. These farms are still vacant. The government should know where these men are. If they are still in industry they should be driven back to the farms to operate them, and the jobs they are occupying should be made available to the returned men.
Farmers in this country have always been the last to get consideration from any legislation, and the first to be penalized. That condition cannot prevail longer. It is the duty of every farm member in this House of Commons to voice his protest against this rise in the price of farm machinery. Every member representing a farming community should voice his protest. If that is done I am not afraid that this increase will be allowed to standi.
Mr. F. W. TOWNLEY-SMITH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my voice to the protest against the proposed

Farm Implements
increase in prices of farm machinery. The farmers have always believed they were being overcharged for their machinery, and I can well imagine the dismay and consternation that will be felt when particularly the western farmers hear of this price increase. I represent an agricultural district, a constituency said to be the largest in the dominion, and I know exactly how these people feel when they come to discuss machinery prices.
The point has been made that an increase in prices of machinery will bring about an increase in the production of the machines. I doubt very much whether that is so. I made application some time ago for some farm machinery, and I have in my possession letters from the manufacturers stating that they are unable to supply what I require. One of these machines is a drill, and my information is that there will not be any drills in the west until June. Well, one can imagine how useful a drill will be in June! If, because of this increase, should it go through, drills are available before that time, it will simply confirm the suspicion in my mind that the whole thing was prearranged and, on the part of somebody, probably the machinery companies, some form of hold-up. I do not believe that point was well taken; as a matter of fact I do not believe it will increase the production of machines.
While we are talking about drills, I should like to make this point. We are told that there has been an increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel. This drill, with certain equipment that I desired on it, was going to cost me in the neighbourhood of $500; it is a big drill. An increase of 12^ per cent would mean something like $62. The drill itself weighs about 1,600 pounds, representing about $4 extra in the cost of the steel, whereas the additional price I shall have to pay will be be some $62. So that I suggest there is really no justification for an argument of that kind.
It is most unfortunate that almost every time agriculture comes under discussion some form of unpleasantness or unhappiness for the farmers seems to result. When I came here * last September one of the first things we talked about in which I was peculiarly interested was the Hudson Bay railway. The improvement of the railroad and the use of the port of Churchill were to be of great advantage to the western farmers, but we completely failed to gain our point. Nothing was done; nothing has been done about the railway or the port. Soon after that, we had an announcement about the price of wheat which, instead of being allowed to follow the world price, was fixed for the time being at $1.55 a bushel. I wonder if hon. members
appreciate just what this price of $1.55 means to me, for instance. They may think I get $1.55 for every bushel of wheat. That is not so. I get as an initial price $1.25, f.o.b. Fort William. At my elevator where I deliver wheat that means to me, if it is No. 1, the best wheat that can be grown, $1.05 a bushel, not $1.55. We hope to get $1.55 eventually, less the charges, but at the present time what I get at my shipping point is $1.05.' Then, shortly after that, meat rationing was ordained, and immediately the price of hogs on the western market slumped $1.25 a hundred, or roughly $2 a pig. After that, coming into this year, the price of gasoline went up two cents, and now we have a suggested increase in farm machinery prices of 12J per cent.
You have already heard, Mr. Speaker, what is happening in the production of butter and the production of hogs. I wonder exactly what the government is trying to do. Butter production is down twenty per cent. Last year the production of hogs was down forty-three per cent, and in my opinion, this year it will be down another twenty-five per cent as far as my province of Saskatchewan is concerned. Yet the need for hogs is very great. The farmers are feeling such irritation, aggravation, disappointment and frustration that they are just about ready to let things go. I wonder if we could warn the government as to what is taking place on those western farms, that the situation is serious and should be carefully considered. In my opinion, a step like this, increasing prices of machinery, is entirely wrong. Last year I tried to make the point that those nations which could grow commodities of quality most economically would get the market; in other words, that those countries which could keep down their production costs would eventually get the world markets. All these things I have been mentioning, the failure to make use of the Hudson Bay line, the price of wheat, the price of machines and so on, mean an increase in production costs and greater difficulty in getting and keeping the markets of the world.
All these matters should be taken into consideration and given careful thought. I hope the minister will reconsider this matter of increasing prices of machinery, because it is an important point. When you are dabbling wdth an industry that grows products to the value of $2,146 million, which are the figures for agriculture for the last year as to which we have available data, it is big business which requires careful handling, for that is a great deal of money. On behalf of my constituency I protest against this increase in
Farm Implements

prices of machinery. It is a most untimely move and an unwise step under any circumstances.

Let us compare that with the financial position of the farmer. The situation of our farmers from 1937 to 1940 was a crime. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) had a little joke about the $2,000 free of income tax for members. I should like to see it raised to $1,200, and the exemption of the married man and his wife raised from $1,250 up to at least $2,400.
I have heard it stated in. the house that eighty-five per cent of the people of Canada work for an income of $1,500 or less. I also see in the press that the finance minister collects half of the total income tax from this eigthy-five per cent.
I feel sure that Canada will be on the way out under this kind of national economy. Where lies the strength of the nation? In good homes, in health and in all these things that make for a prosperous countryside. How is the boy who is just starting up going to get

anywhere with an income tax exemption of only $660, or the man who is trying to build a home? How can the boys who are coming back buy a- farm and pay for farm implements at these increased prices? How are they ever going to get started? LTsing the simple logic of a simple farmer, I would say that this Canada of ours is on the way out and that it will not take long to get there if you impoverish rural Canada, the source of all supplies. This is a matter of the greatest importance, and I should like to see the government give it its most serious consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time has perhaps come when I should answer some of the statements that have been made in the numerous speeches to-day. I do not hope to be able to deal with all the numerous speeches, but I wish to clear up some misconceptions that are in the minds of hon. members and to answer some questions that have been asked.
One aspect of the discussion, that is gratifying is the support that now comes from most members of the house for the principle of price control. At least it seems to be popular. We started a general price ceiling in 1941 and at the same time instituted a system of wage stabilization. We had an- uphill fight to have the principle of over-all price control accepted by the Canadian people, either by agriculture or by labour. As the years went on, perhaps the wisdom of our policy became more apparent, and when recently it became obvious that if we w7ere to avoid a complete break-down of price control and wage stabilization there must be some yielding in some places, we discovered that when and to the extent that we yielded at all we met with tremendous protest. I have tried on several occasions to explain to this house that it is utterly impossible to maintain indefinitely rigid price control. To begin with, we have to get out of this field constitutionally some time; we have not the power to stay in this field indefinitely, and there must be a certain amount of decontrol. This was explained on numerous occasions.
As I understood the position taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) this afternoon, he said that if this authorization of a raising of the price ceiling on agricultural implements w'as necessary, it was in the wrong order, that other ceilings should be raised first, the ceilings on agricultural products, or on wages, or on both: I think he mentioned both wages and prices of agricultural products. Other speakers said that we had put the cart before the horse. I want to point out that we have not put the cart before the

Farm Implements
horse. Both with regard to wages and with regard to farm prices there have been repeated and extensive upward adjustments from 1941 down to the present time.
First, with regard to wages, one of the reasons why there has to be an upward adjustment of the ceiling on farm implements at the present time is the increase in wages in the farm implement industry. I said in my statement this afternoon that wages in this industry had increased by 281 per cent. I was asked by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) whether it is true that in the agricultural impfement industry in Toronto wages had been reduced and some of the men had been laid off. I made inquiries between six and eight o'clock, and I find that the western plant of the Massey-Harris company, which was engaged on war production, has been closed, and that the war workers were given the option of transferring their activities to the agricultural implement plant, where the wages may have been lower than in the war plant, but that there has been no reduction whatever in agricultural implement wages. As a matter of fact, the increase in wages paid by the Massey-Harris company, according to information which I have obtained, is as follows: 1939, 511 cents an hour; 1941, 59-7 cents an hour; 1945, 79-4 cents an hour; 1946, about 80 cents an hour is the average present wage rate of the employees of that company. This indicates a wage increase of approximately 331 per cent. With regard to wages generally in Canada- and I say this on the point that the government has put the cart before the horse, and in rebuttal of the accusation that the government meets the wishes of big business, or business generally, before it meets the demands of labour and agriculture-I wish to point out that, according to the Department of Labour figures, the average hourly wage rates in all industries in 1944 were forty-four per cent above the average of 1935-39 and eighteen per cent above 1941. I say that because some hon. members have gone rather far in stating that I as Minister of Finance am particularly amenable to the appeals of business, or big business, rather than those of other classes in the community. That is not so, nor is it true of the wartime prices and trade board. The whole record and history of the wartime prices and trade board shows that it is consumer-minded. There is not anybody in Canada who knows anything about the record of the wartime prices and trade board and has followed it through the years who can deny that it is consumer-minded. So much so, that it has been [DOT]denounced at times by agriculture; it has
been denounced at times by labour; it has been accused of being obsessed with the idea that we must have low wages and low prices in this country. I do- not think the wartime prices and trade board has gone too far, but it has been accused of going too far along those lines, and certainly nobody can deny that the first and paramount interest of the wartime prices and trade board is the interest of the consumer, which in this case is the farmer consumer.
We have to leave these matters to somebody. The government cannot conduct the exhaustive investigations which are necessary to bring to light every detail in these investigations. The body which has been set up to consider what prices are proper under the circumstances is the wartime prices and trade board. I have faith in that board because I have worked with it over the last five or six years, and there is one thing I know they will not do; I know they will not authorize a price increase unless that price increase is absolutely necessary. The reason that a price increase was authorized in this case was because of the great cost increases.
I said a few minutes ago that there had been repeated upward adjustments in prices of agricultural products. I must, I think, place on record some of the increases which have taken place, in prices of agricultural products since 1941, merely by way of reply to the charge that we do not meet other groups but meet the claims of business. I am not saying for one minute that the increases were excessive. I am not saying for one minute that price increases over the level of the fall of 1941 were not desirable, because the price level before the war was low, and while it rose somewhat between 1939 and the fall of 1941 it did not rise as high as it should have. But since 1941-and these are figures given by the bureau of statistics- average prices of farm products, including subsidies, in 1945 as compared with average prices for 1941 showed the following increases: wheat, 67 per cent, or, if an estimated participation of fifteen cents be included, 87 per cent; oats 65 per cent, barley 62 per cent, hogs 51 per cent. The recent adjustments in hog prices would increase this to 70 per cent. Cattle, 40 per cent; fluid milk, 28 per cent; butter, 29 per cent; with the recent price increase, 40 per cent; cheese, 53 per cent; eggs, 28 per cent; potatoes, 135 per cent; all [DOT] farm prices, 48 per cent, farm machinery, three per cent.

subtopic: INCREASE IN RETAIL PRICE CEILINGS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
That is one objection to the suggestion that sounded reasonable to-day, and is reasonable in principle, that before you change any ceiling you ought to have a public hearing. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) put that forward very strongly. If we were to have changes in the ceilings taking place all the time-they have been taking place all the time over the last two or three years, and they are taking place more rapidly recently-it would be utterly impossible from the administrative point of view to have public hearings on all these price changes. If we selected some of the more important ones-I was thinking about this as I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver East for whom I need hardly say I have much respect-I do not know where we would stop. Each person who was heard would say: "Well, I am entitled to a public hearing on this matter." It would have to be advertised and so on. But it seems to me there is this big difference between a price hearing and a wage hearing. In the case of a wage hearing the wage increase, if it is eventually granted, may be dated back to the time of the application and very often is. The price increase cannot. If you had a hearing that lasted as long as some of the wage hearings have lasted, and if you had a price hearing on this matter that lasted several months you could not, of course, date the price back. Therefore, if you had a situation where the producer of the article really needed the increase in order to operate you could not do anything effective for him at all. The suggestion that there should be public hearings is impracticable. We have to have faith in the wartime prices and trade board. Their record and their outlook have been such that, however much people desiring higher prices may dislike them-and they have taken a great deal of abuse all through the years from people who desire higher prices-those who desire low prices, prices as low as can be maintained, can trust them.
These were some of the questions that were brought up this afternoon. One other question was asked by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Menary), namely, what happened in the case of an article which

was purchased before the effective date of the increase in the price ceiling? I made inquiries and attempted to get the information in that regard. The increase came into effect on April 13. If a man has a contract for delivery the ordinary law of contract applies; but if a sale takes place on or after the 13th day of April the vendor may sell at the new price.
There is one point which perhaps I ought to make clear. After listening to a number of the speeches this afternoon, one would1 have thought the government was raising these prices. The order of the wartime prices and trade board does not raise the prices; it merely authorizes an increase in prices, raises the ceiling on the prices. The circumstances at the present time are such that the producers can take advantage of that. We removed the duty from agricultural implements; we removed the war exchange tax and so on from agricultural implements, so that no advantage whatever can be taken of the tariff. We get the advantage of the competitive United States market, to the extent that it is an advantage, and I presume it is of some. The tone of some of the speeches was that we were just going in and saying, "You have to pay these increased prices." We are just removing the control of the prices to that extent, raising the ceilings to the extent of 12% per cent.
I have a great deal more material here, Mr. Speaker, but I do not know that there is very much more I could usefully add.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of making one or two brief observations and a suggestion. The suggestion is not wholly new; it is very similar to the one made by the hon. member' for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). The reason I do that is this. It seems to me that it is important not only to do what is believed to be the right thing but to make people believe it is the right thing. If anything were needed to support the statement made this afternoon by my leader that this matter was not carried out as well as it might have been, it is the debate we have had; when we have seen what, to a new member like myself at any rate, seems an unprecedented spate of protest against what the government is doing.	.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) has made a statement to which we have all listened with respect. Personally I would not presume to disagree with it because I do not know enough about the facts. On the other hand, we have had a great many people here who do disagree with it, and so I come to this. I agree with what has been said that it is in the highest degree unfortunate that a decision of this kind has to be arrived at by methods fair-minded men have to-day described as in camera, secretly, and so on. I fully realize the force of the minister's statement that we cannot have a debate in parliament on every 63260-57
decision that has to be made, but nonetheless I suggest that there are certain basic principles underlying the de-controls which must come within the next few months. So that I submit for the consideration of the minister and the government whether it would not be possible to have some body, I do not know whether it should be the agriculture committee, the banking and commerce committee or a combination of the two if you wish, which would ask to appear before it people who are supposed to have competent opinions on these important questions, which I recognize as very difficult, and to ask also representatives of labour, of the farmers, of the manufacturers and of all the other people interested. The minister may say, "Oh, well, you would just have a kind of debate which would lead to nothing." I am not suggesting that, this body could proceed to decide on this and this and this de-control in Gatling-gun fashion, but I suggest that at the present time there is a great deal of misapprehension in the public mind, and that if we are to have merely one announcement after another that this and this and this has been . de-controlled, it is not the best way of trying to get across to the public mind what, it seems to me, it is so enormously important that we should get into the public mind.
The thing that has distressed me to-day and harrassed my mind beyond words is the statement we have heard in this house as to farms abandoned, as to people unwilling to leave the cities to go to work on the farms. I heard a figure as to the percentage of men who had come from farms and were now unwilling to go back to them, which was so high I simply could not credit it; nevertheless there is the problem. It seems to me one of enormous importance, and therefore with great respect, not with any desire to complicate this difficult question but because I believe at the present time it is not being really met, I offer this suggestion. I believe the debate we have had to-day shows that the problem is not being met, when once there is this widespread measure of protest. I realize that the protests come from farming constituencies. I represent one myself, though it will be observed that I have not made a protest. Nevertheless I feel there are basic principles here which might well be discussed in open forum, so that the citizens of Canada might have a better understanding than they now have of the problems and the basic principles which are to be followed in dealing with the matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was suggested

Farm Implements

a few minutes ago that it might be necessary for one of the members of the opposition to speak for the Minister of Agriculture. I think it is pretty well understood, however, that I usually speak for myself.
There are one or two reasons why it would be necessary for me to say something in a debate of this kind. The first is that I do not think that in the ten years I have been here I have allowed a debate on a question involving an increase in the price of farm implements to go by without my saying something. If I were to do so on this occasion it might be misunderstood.
In addition to that, like many other hon. members I intend to go to my constituency during the Easter recess, and I am certain again that if I did not express myself upon this question I might be misunderstood there -and I have seldom allowed myself to be misunderstood in my own constituency.
Another reason for my rising is that one or two of the suggestions made require a little analysis. We have talked a great deal this afternoon and this evening about a 12^ per cent increase in the price of farm implements. I think I am as much opposed as anyone in Canada-and every farmer is opposed-to an increase in the price of farm implements, believing as I do and as most farmers do, as has been stated a number of times this afternoon, that farm implement prices, if anything, have always been a little too high. So that one has to have proven to him the fact that they are 'as low as they ought to be, in order to be entirely satisfied.
But on this occasion perhaps too great emphasis has been given to the increase of 12j per cent, and more particularly by my hon. friends directly opposite, in view of the statement I have heard them make on many previous occasions. Each time that I have been attempting to prove that we should have lower prices for farm implements, I have always been told that it does not involve more than from three to six per cent of the farmer's cost of production. I think the report that was read this afternoon on so many occasions bears that out-and probably accepts the higher figure of six per cent. If that is true, what we have been talking about this afternoon is three-quarters of one per cent of the farmer's cost of production, when we speak of a 12^ per cent increase. I wish to make that statement only in order to have the record straight in so far as what we actually do is concerned.
If there were no other considerations I would think that even three-quarters of one [Mr. Gardiner. 1
per cent of an increase in farm costs of production at the present time would be a most important matter, and that it should be justified on some ground or another. I consider the statement made a few minutes ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) was a very fair statement of the relationship between farmers and the implement industry, and a very fair statement in respect of what has happened since 1941 to the farmers as compared with what has happened to the farm implement companies.
But I wish to emphasize a little more

and he emphasized it-the fact that these increases, so far as the farmers are concerned, began at a very low level, and did advance eventually to a fairly high level. Considered, of course, in terms of percentages, that can be represented in very high figures.
There is another argument which is being used in the country, but which was not used in the house this afternoon. I wish to refer to it because it has been used in the country, and more particularly in some of the financial papers. The suggestion has been made that farmers are very well off. I do not find any more common statement. Indeed I find it quite often in the corridors of this building- the statement to the effect that farmers are well off. Because of that statement being made, we have been arriving at conclusions which are not justified by the facts.
One of the most apparent reasons for making the statement is contained in a table which has been issued, indicating the extent to which farmers have paid off their indebtedness for farm machinery, and on mortgages. I was just reading this evening one statement which indicated that thirty mortgage companies in Canada-and some hon. members opposite know very well the records of some of them- had had the indebtedness of farmers reduced by S102 million. That is, early in the war the indebtedness of those farmers was $168 million, while at the end of the war or last year, it was down to $66 million.
I should just like to make an analysis of what that means. It certainly does not mean that the farmer has $100 million more in cash. It does mean that farm-era have worked hard for long days during the years of this war to produce products which have been sold at reasonable prices under arrangements made through the wartime prices and trade board. They have worked long hours and long days, and by doing so have accumulated $100 million which has been paid into the treasuries of thirty loan companies in Canada.
That is a partial job well done. They still owe $66 million. Any man or any group of

Farm Implements
men which still owes any debt, particularly a group owing $66 million to thirty mortgage companies, is not yet well off. That statement ought to be emphasized. Until that other $66 million is paid off, the farmers who owe that money are not well off. Every farmer in this country, or every farmer who farms in this country, knows that a farmer has only one ambition, if he is ever going to be well off, and that is to have his farm clear of deist. His second ambition is to have his farm implements clear of debt.
If any farmer in this country with an average, family-sized farm, has his farm clear of debt, and his implements and stock clear of debt, then I venture to say on the floor of this house that there is not any nicer way of living than living on the farm. But if the farmer is loaded down with debt, even to the extent of a few thousand dollars, it is hard for him to make a living on the farm, with people Phasing after him from morning to night to get him to pay his debts. That farmer will not have a very comfortable time on the farm, nor will he enjoy working there.
So that, I think, while he has taken off $102 million from a debt of $168 million owed to some thirty mortgage companies-and owing a great deal more in some other directions-that we should pay attention to that fact, when considering his present position, rather than pay attention only to the fact that he has paid off- that amount of debt.
There is one other point I wish to make, and it is this: As the Minister of Finance , pointed out, we have made recently some increases in farm prices. There has been an increase in the price of butter of four cents which, after all, is an increase of ten per cent. It is not three-quarters of one per cent, and it might be fair to compare it with the 12i per cent increase to implement Companies. But to the farmers who produce butter it is an increase of ten per cent. In both cases it is an increase on top of the price at which he was probably at least getting by prior to getting that increase. So that I am sure it is acknowledged in the country as a very helpful increase; at least' it is as much as the organized farmers asked for.
The other increase which was made was the six per cent increase on hogs. Many of us are going home to our constituencies during the Easter recess, and many of those constituencies are agricultural. I am speaking as a member of the government because there are only two of us on this side from Saskatchewan and I think any message we have to give out should go to that province, namely, 63260-57$	*
that the prices board cannot make all its adjustments at once unless it is prepared to agree that the position taken by the official opposition is the correct one, that we should make all our decisions at once to close the whole thing up. If that were the case, then, of course, you could make all your adjustments at once. But barring that, there is only one other way, and that is to do it partly, one at a time; then work along with the job until finally you have it completed. I am confident whether other members of the house are or not, and I am going to exercise any ability that I have to spread that confidence, that the adjustments which have been made will be followed up by more adjustments. I am also satisfied and confident that when those adjustments are all made, a good job will have been done and that our farming population can at least during the next few years proceed to pay off the remainder of the debt. When they have that debt paid off I hope we shall be able to say that the farmer is well off. Because for Canada to be well off, the farmer must be well off. When he is well off, others are well off in common with him. Then we shall be able to go back to our constituencies, wherever they may be, and say that we have taken some part in doing a job that will be of some assistance to this country.

What is the alternative? We do not want to vote the government out of power. The purpose of the motion has been achieved. A good discussion has been had; protests have been made, and the minister has made' his answer. That is a good thing for Canada. The difficulty was, Mr. Speaker, that prior to this time decisions were made outside this house, and then the minister would come in and explain them under conditions where there could not be any debate; That is what I protested chiefly against to-day. Our protests have now been made and the minister has made his answer, and better than he ever did before in any statement he has made. I think the purpose of the motion has been achieved and, as is customary under such conditions, I ask leave to withdraw the motion.
